    Summary and Schedule

    Intro to Programming, Part 1 is the first of two six-week, beginner Python micro-credentials from the Australian Data and Cyber Institute (ADCI). Part 2 is a separate course. It is for complete beginners, especially people in office jobs who want to change career or move into programming or computing. You do not need any programming or technical background. Each week takes 6 hours or less, so it fits around a full-time job, and the course is designed to support credit towards an introductory programming unit.

    You learn mostly from short YouTube videos (the Telusko Python for Beginners playlist, plus a few videos from other channels), these lesson notes, and a practice task each week. You write and run all the code in PyCharm.

    Learning outcomes

    By the end of the six weeks you will be able to:

    • LO 1 Analyse and solve a problem, and implement the solution in a programming language.
    • LO 2 Apply object-oriented, imperative, functional and logic programming techniques.
    • LO 3 Design and build a small program to meet a given specification.
    • LO 4 Evaluate which programming paradigm best suits a particular problem.

    How each week works

    Each week is one episode in the menu. Open a week to see its parts: the week overview, the sections (such as 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3), the Concepts Bridge and the practice task. Every week follows the same blocks:

    Block Time What you do
    Watch about 0.3 to 1.25 h Short videos listed on the week overview
    Read & practise about 1 to 2 h The week’s sections: read, run every example, do the exercises
    Concepts Bridge 30 min General programming ideas the Python lessons do not cover
    Build 2 h (3 h in Week 6) Your portfolio item: a practice task with starter code, a model solution and tests
    Quiz 15 min A short quiz, marked automatically

    Your portfolio for each week is submitted at the end of the week and marked by your tutor.

    Prerequisite

    Prerequisites

    • No programming experience is needed.
    • A computer (Windows, Mac or Linux) where you can install software.
    • Follow the Setup page before Week 1.
    Setup Instructions Download files required for the lesson
    Duration: 00h 00m  1. Week 1: Getting started: how programs run, values and operators What will I learn in Week 1, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    What is Python and why is it a good first language?
    How do I run Python code in the shell and in a file?
    How do I store values so I can use them again?
    Which functions come built into Python?
    How does Python do arithmetic?
    How do I compare values and combine conditions?
    How does a program take in information, work on it and give a result?
    Can I combine input, variables and operators in a small program?
    Duration: 05h 40m  2. Week 2: Input and data structures What will I learn in Week 2, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    How do I store many values in order and change them?
    When should I use a tuple instead of a list?
    How do I keep only unique values and compare groups?
    How do I store values that I look up by name?
    Which data structure should I use for a job?
    Can I use a dictionary of lists to manage real data?
    Duration: 10h 50m  3. Week 3: Control flow and functions What will I learn in Week 3, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    How can a program choose what to do?
    How do I repeat steps without copying code?
    How do I write code once and reuse it?
    How do I plan a solution before I code it?
    Can I plan and build a program with functions and decisions?
    Duration: 16h 30m  4. Week 4: Recursion, functional programming and errors What will I learn in Week 4, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    How can I build lists in one line?
    What is a lambda function?
    How can functions work with other functions?
    What do Python error messages mean?
    How can my program keep going when something goes wrong?
    What are programming paradigms?
    How do functional and logic programming differ from what I have done so far?
    How does a functional version of a program compare with an imperative one?
    Duration: 21h 53m  5. Week 5: Object-oriented programming What will I learn in Week 5, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    How do I create my own data types?
    What does “everything is an object” mean?
    What is a dunder method?
    Can I model real things with classes?
    Duration: 02h 38m  6. Week 6: Modules and choosing a paradigm What will I learn in Week 6, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    How do I split code into files and use code others have written?
    How do I choose a paradigm for a problem?
    Can I finish a complete program and justify its design?
    Duration: 07h 32m Finish

    The actual schedule may vary slightly depending on the topics and exercises chosen by the instructor.

    You need two free programs: Python (the language) and PyCharm (the editor you write code in). Section 1.1 walks through both installs; this page is a short checklist.

    Software Setup

    Discussion

    What you will install

    • Python 3.12 or newer from python.org.
    • PyCharm from jetbrains.com/pycharm. Since version 2025.1 there is one PyCharm download; its core features are free. Ignore the Pro trial if you are offered one: everything in this course works in the free core.

    Video help: Telusko T#2 Python Installation, PyCharm (9:33). The PyCharm download page in the video is older, so it looks a little different.

    1. Download Python from python.org and run the installer.
    2. On the first screen, tick Add python.exe to PATH, then choose Install Now.
    3. Open Command Prompt and type python --version. You should see Python 3.12 or newer.
    4. Download and install PyCharm with the default options.
    1. Download the macOS installer from python.org and run it.
    2. Open Terminal and type python3 --version. You should see Python 3.12 or newer.
    3. Download PyCharm (choose Apple Silicon or Intel to match your Mac) and drag it into Applications.
    1. Most Linux systems already have Python 3. Check with python3 --version; if it is older than 3.12, install a newer version with your package manager.
    2. Install PyCharm from the JetBrains website or with JetBrains Toolbox.

    Create your course folder

    1. Create a folder called IntroToProgramming in your Documents folder.
    2. In PyCharm choose File > Open and open that folder.
    3. Create one .py file per section, for example section_1_2.py, and click the green arrow to run it.

    Data Sets

    Some lessons open data files such as data/countries.py or files/example.txt. Download the course data zip file and unzip it into your Documents folder. It gives you an IntroToProgramming folder with:

    • a data folder: countries lists, speeches, a weight and height CSV and more;
    • a files folder: small text, CSV, JSON and XML files for Section 5.2.

    Each week’s practice task lists its own starter files to download.
